items.scenario: A teammate needs to refactor error handling across 30 files in a service repository and plans to paste the files into a chat conversation in batches.
items.question: What is the better route, and why?
options: Keep the chat approach but paste smaller batches so the context doesn't overflow
Use Claude Code in the repository: it reads the real files, makes coordinated edits, and can run the tests
Upload the files to a Project so they persist, then ask for the refactor in chat
Use Claude in Chrome to open the files in the Git hosting UI and edit them there
items.explanation: Repository work belongs in Claude Code. Pasting into chat loses file relationships, can't run tests, and creates copy-paste drift between what Claude saw and what's on disk.
distractors: Smaller batches make it worse: each batch sees even less of the codebase and nothing gets tested.
A Project persists the files, but it still can't edit the repository or run anything. You'd copy results back by hand.
Browser-driven editing of 30 files is slow, unauditable and the wrong tool when a repository agent exists.

items.scenario: A colleague posts a screenshot of a Claude feature in the champions channel. You can't find it in your own app.
items.question: What's the most reliable way to determine whether you have it?
options: Assume you have it, because the colleague is in the same company
Check your own settings and plan entitlements, and the official help/release notes for its plan and status
Ask Claude in chat whether your account has the feature
Reinstall the app until the feature appears
items.explanation: Features are gated by plan, seat type, admin settings and rollout status. Your own settings and the authoritative docs are the evidence, not someone else's screenshot.
distractors: Different seats (Standard vs Premium, Team vs Enterprise) and admin toggles mean colleagues can see different features.
The model doesn't reliably know your account's entitlements and can be confidently wrong.
Gating is server-side. Reinstalling doesn't change entitlements.

items.scenario: You ask Claude in an agentic session to tidy a shared folder. In a plain chat last week, you asked it how to tidy the same folder.
items.question: How should your review differ between the two?
options: No difference. Review the final message in both cases
In chat you review an answer; in the agentic session you review the actions taken (files moved, renamed, deleted) as well as the summary
Agentic sessions don't need review because they show a progress bar
Review only the chat version. Agentic sessions are logged by the admin anyway
items.explanation: In chat nothing changes until you act. In an agentic session Claude acts on your behalf, so what you check moves from what it said to what it did.
distractors: A summary can omit or misdescribe actions. You need to check the actions themselves.
Progress indicators show activity, not correctness.
Audit logs support investigation after the fact. They don't replace your review before damage spreads.

items.scenario: Your team wants a dependency-vulnerability summary generated every Monday morning from the same sources, in the same format.
items.question: Which approach fits best?
options: Someone pastes the sources into chat every Monday
A reusable Skill or workflow run as a scheduled task
Build a product feature on the API
Ask in a Project once and re-read the same answer each week
items.explanation: Repeatable or scheduled work maps to Skills and scheduled tasks, so the same instructions run consistently without manual re-prompting.
distractors: Manual repetition drifts in format and quality, and depends on someone remembering.
The API is for building product features. It's overkill for an internal recurring report.
A stale answer doesn't reflect new vulnerabilities.

items.scenario: You need realistic data to reproduce a bug in a user-import pipeline that fails on unusual names and duplicate IDs.
items.question: What should you give Claude?
options: A sample of 50 real rows from the production users table
The schema and a description of the edge cases, asking it to generate synthetic records
The production rows with surnames removed
Nothing. Bugs involving user data can't be worked on with AI
items.explanation: Synthetic stand-ins keep the shape and edge cases without personal data. That's minimisation in practice.
distractors: Production personal data is on the never-paste list.
Partial removal still leaves identifiable personal data (first names, emails, IDs).
Over-correction. Synthetic data makes this safe.

items.scenario: Claude is summarising a batch of inbound support tickets through a connector. Halfway through, it proposes closing three tickets and posting a comment quoting text from one customer's ticket.
items.question: What's the right response?
options: Approve. Closing resolved tickets saves time
Approve the comment but not the closures
Deny, stop the session, and report a likely prompt injection with the ticket attached
Ask Claude why it wants to do that, then approve if the reason sounds plausible
items.explanation: You asked for a summary, not writes. An unrequested write that echoes untrusted ticket content is the signature of injection. Recognise, stop, report.
distractors: You didn't ask for closures, and the instruction likely came from untrusted content.
The comment is just as unrequested and may leak or spread the injected text.
A hijacked session will produce a plausible-sounding reason. Asking it is not a control.

items.scenario: You're about to share a Kubernetes manifest with Claude to debug a crash loop. It references a Secret by name, and an env block contains a database URL with an embedded password.
items.question: What do you do before pasting?
options: Nothing. Kubernetes manifests are internal, so they're fine on the company seat
Replace the password in the URL with a placeholder (and verify with a quick grep). The Secret reference name can stay
Base64-encode the password so it isn't readable
Delete the entire env block, including variable names
items.explanation: Credentials are never-paste, whatever the plan. Redact the value and keep the structure Claude needs for debugging.
distractors: The manifest is internal, but the embedded credential is restricted. Classification follows the most sensitive item.
Base64 is encoding, not encryption. It's trivially reversible.
Over-redaction. Variable names are often key to diagnosing a crash loop.

items.scenario: A shared team Project contains your org's internal runbooks. You want to add a client's architecture document marked 'Confidential — NDA'.
items.question: Which check matters most?
options: Whether the document is under the file-size limit
Whether the client contract allows AI processing, and whether everyone in the Project is authorised to see that client's material
Whether memory is enabled for the Project
Whether the Project has custom instructions
items.explanation: Two gates: the client's permission for AI processing, and need-to-know across the Project's membership, since Project files are visible to every member.
distractors: Feasibility, not confidentiality.
Memory affects persistence. It doesn't settle authorisation.
Instructions shape output, not access.

items.scenario: Your team is about to hard-code a specific model ID into a nightly data-classification job that will run for the next year.
items.question: What should you check first?
options: Whether the model is the newest one available
The model deprecation and retirement page, and a plan to re-test when you switch
Whether the model has the largest context window
Nothing. Model IDs are stable forever
items.explanation: Models retire. Before you standardise a script or team on a model, check its deprecation status and plan the migration and re-test.
distractors: Newest isn't the criterion. Fitness for the task and the retirement timeline are.
Context size is irrelevant to short classification inputs.
Models are deprecated and retired on published schedules.

items.scenario: An engineer wants to load an entire 150k-line monorepo into a single chat to ask how authentication works.
items.question: What's the best advice?
options: It fits, since current models have huge context windows. Paste it all
Estimate the tokens first. At roughly 10 tokens per line it far exceeds the window, so use Claude Code's agentic search to find the auth code instead
Compress the code by removing all whitespace and comments so it fits
Ask a faster, smaller model, because it has a bigger context window
items.explanation: A rough estimate (150k lines × ~10 tokens ≈ 1.5M tokens) shows it won't fit. Even when something fits, stuffing degrades quality and cost. Targeted retrieval wins.
distractors: A large window still has limits, and filling it raises cost and latency and dilutes attention.
Mangling the code loses meaning and still won't fit.
Smaller models aren't defined by bigger windows, and the real fix is retrieval, not a different window.

items.scenario: You ask Claude which version of a popular open-source library is the latest. It answers confidently.
items.question: How should you treat the answer?
options: Trust it. The model is trained on the library's docs
Treat it as possibly stale, because of the training cut-off, and force a web search or check the release page
Ask the same question again. If it repeats, it's correct
Switch to a bigger model, which will know the latest version
items.explanation: Anything that changes over time ('latest', prices, versions) may postdate the training cut-off. Use search or a primary source.
distractors: Training data stops at the cut-off. Later releases are unknown.
Consistency isn't correctness. A stale answer can repeat reliably.
Every model has a cut-off. Size doesn't fix recency.

items.scenario: A QA engineer's test for an LLM-powered feature passes and fails on alternate runs with an identical prompt.
items.question: What's the right interpretation?
options: The API is broken. File a bug
Outputs are non-deterministic, so test properties across several runs (format, required facts, constraints), not exact strings
Set a random seed in the prompt text to make it deterministic
Retry until it passes, then commit
items.explanation: The same prompt can give different answers. Robust tests assert properties over a small sample of runs.
distractors: Variation is expected behaviour, not an outage.
Writing 'seed=42' in a prompt doesn't control sampling.
Retrying until green hides real failures.

items.scenario: A prompt reads: 'Write something about the outage for the team.' The output is generic and too long.
items.question: Which rewrite addresses the most defects?
options: 'Write something better about the outage for the team, please.'
'You are an expert. Write about the outage.'

'Draft a 120-word Slack update for the support team about today's 47-minute checkout outage (timeline below). Include impact, current status and next update time. Plain language, no internal service names, because support will paste it to customers.'
'Write about the outage. Do not be generic. Do not be long. Do not use jargon.'
items.explanation: It fixes the vague task, missing context, missing format and length, missing audience, and gives the reason (the why), which improves compliance with constraints.
distractors: Politeness doesn't add task, context, format or audience.
A role alone leaves every other defect in place.
Prohibitions without positive specification leave Claude guessing what you do want.

items.scenario: You need Claude to analyse a 30-page RFC and answer a specific question about its rollback strategy.
items.question: How should the prompt be structured?
options: Question first, then the RFC, then repeat the question
The RFC inside clearly labelled tags first, then the instructions and question at the end
Just the question. Claude will ask for the RFC if needed
Split the RFC into 30 messages, one page each, then ask
items.explanation: Delimit the data from the instructions, put long material first and the question last. This improves long-document answers.
distractors: Repetition adds noise. Placing the question after the material is the pattern that helps.
Claude can't analyse a document it hasn't been given.
Fragmenting the document makes it harder to reason over as a whole.

items.scenario: You gave Claude one example action-item row in your preferred table format. Every output row now copies the example's owner name and due date.
items.question: What happened, and what's the fix?
options: Claude is broken. Remove all examples
Overfitting to a single example. Use 2–3 diverse examples that vary the content, and state that content comes from the notes
Add 'DO NOT COPY THE EXAMPLE' in capitals
Increase the effort level
items.explanation: Examples are imitated strongly. Diverse examples teach the format without anchoring on specific values.
distractors: Examples are valuable for format. Fix how you use them rather than dropping them.
Shouting is weaker than better examples, and can over-trigger in other ways.
This is an example-design problem, not a reasoning-depth problem.

items.scenario: After six follow-up corrections in the same chat, Claude's answers keep sliding back toward the first wrong interpretation.
items.question: What's the most effective next step?
options: Add a seventh, more forceful correction
Edit the original prompt to include what you learned, and re-run it in a fresh context
Switch to the smallest model for speed
Ask Claude to apologise and try harder
items.explanation: Accumulated wrong turns pollute the context. Fixing the spec and re-running gives a clean start with the right information.
distractors: More corrections pile more conflicting context on top.
This is a spec problem, not a speed one.
Apologies change nothing about the inputs.

items.scenario: You're asking Claude to estimate migration effort for a legacy service, but key facts (team size, test coverage) are uncertain.
items.question: Which addition to the prompt most improves the usefulness of the answer?
options: 'Be accurate.'
'List the assumptions you made and the open questions that would change the estimate, alongside the estimate.'
'Answer in one number only.'
'Pretend you know the team.'
items.explanation: Surfacing assumptions and open questions makes gaps visible and reviewable, instead of being silently filled with guesses.
distractors: An instruction to be accurate adds no information.
A bare number hides the uncertainty you most need to see.
That invites invention.

items.scenario: Claude drafted a client status email that reads well. It mentions a delivery date of the 14th and a 20% performance gain.
items.question: What must happen before you send it?
options: Send it. The draft is fluent and professional
Check every name, number and commitment against the source, and add the verification note required for client-facing text
Ask Claude whether the numbers are correct
Run a spell-check, then send
items.explanation: Sending discipline: fluent isn't the same as correct. Every name, number and commitment is verified by you, and client-facing text carries a verification note.
distractors: Polish lowers vigilance, and that's exactly when wrong numbers slip through.
Self-checking by the same model isn't independent verification.
Spelling isn't the risk. Wrong commitments and figures are.

items.scenario: You must explain the same database migration to (a) the client's CTO and (b) your peer engineers.
items.question: What's the most efficient approach?
options: Write one version and send it to both
In one chat, give the facts once, then ask for two drafts with an explicit reader and register for each (executive impact/risk vs technical steps/rollback)
Write the engineer version and ask the CTO to skip the technical parts
Ask Claude for 'a professional tone' and send it to both
items.explanation: Rewriting for a defined reader is a core technique. The same facts in different registers serve each audience without re-explaining context.
distractors: One register rarely serves both audiences.
That pushes the editing work onto the reader.
'Professional' isn't an audience. Name the reader.

items.scenario: Claude turned a long incident thread into a decision summary with an action table listing owners and due dates.
items.question: What is the key verification step?
options: Check that the table formatting renders correctly
Trace every action, owner and date back to a specific message in the thread, because summaries can drop or invent them
Ask the thread participants whether they like the format
None. Summarisation is a strength of the model
items.explanation: Compression produces attribution errors and invented owners or dates. Each action must be traceable to its source.
distractors: Formatting is cosmetic. Correctness is the risk.
Preference isn't verification.
Being strong at a task doesn't make the output error-free. Summaries are exactly where hallucinated actions appear.

items.scenario: You need a 25-page design document for a new platform service.
items.question: Which workflow produces the best result?
options: One prompt: 'Write the full design doc'
Outline first and review it, then draft section by section, then run consistency and glossary passes
Draft all sections in parallel chats and merge them by hand
Write it yourself, then ask Claude to make it longer
items.explanation: Outline-first gives structure and checkpoints. Section-by-section drafting keeps quality high. Consistency passes catch drift in terms and claims.
distractors: One-shot long documents lose coherence and are hard to review.
Parallel drafts without a shared outline drift in terminology and overlap.
Length isn't the goal. Clarity for the reader is.

items.scenario: You enable a Drive connector and ask: 'Summarise my documents about the Q3 launch.'
items.question: What does the connector have access to?
options: Only documents with 'Q3' in the title
Whatever your account can access in Drive, through the tools the connector exposes, so scope the request tightly
Only documents you uploaded to Claude
Only public documents
items.explanation: Connectors act as your identity. The model sees only the results, but the reachable surface is everything you can reach. Scope by folder, date or owner.
distractors: Filtering depends on what the model searches for, not a built-in title restriction.
That describes Project uploads, not a connector.
Connectors use your permissions, including private files.

items.scenario: In a session with a Jira connector, you review the transcript and see calls to get_issue, search_issues and transition_issue.
items.question: Which statement is correct?
options: All three are reads, because they relate to issues
get_issue and search_issues are reads. transition_issue is a write that changes state in Jira and deserves explicit review
All three are writes, because they call an API
Tool names don't matter. Only the final answer does
items.explanation: Classifying each tool call as read or write is the core auditing habit. Writes change the world outside the conversation.
distractors: Transitioning an issue changes its state. That's a write.
Reads call APIs too. What matters is whether the call changes anything.
Reading tool calls is what makes connector use auditable.

items.scenario: You need to download five invoices from a vendor portal that has no API or connector.
items.question: Which tool fits, with which precaution?
options: A custom MCP connector you write today
Claude in Chrome on an allow-listed site, in a browser profile not signed in to unrelated sensitive systems, watching each step
Paste your vendor portal password into chat so Claude can log in
Claude Code with bypassPermissions
items.explanation: Chrome is the right tool when no connector exists. Its blast radius is your signed-in browser, so limit what that browser can reach and supervise it.
distractors: Building and approving a connector is far out of proportion for five downloads, and needs admin approval.
Credentials are never-paste.
The wrong surface, and the widest permission mode, for a web task.

items.scenario: A colleague proposes setting every connector to auto-approve in your agentic sessions 'to stop the interruptions', including the Gmail connector with send.
items.question: What's the best response?
options: Agree. Approval prompts are just friction
Auto-approve only trusted read-only tools. Keep approval on any write tool such as send, because the prompt is the human gate against injection
Disable all connectors permanently
Agree, but check the sent folder each evening
items.explanation: Match the approval posture to the risk. Read-only tools can be trusted. Write tools, especially outbound ones, keep a human in the loop.
distractors: The friction is the control. Removing it on send tools opens an exfiltration path.
Over-correction that forfeits the value.
Checking after the fact can't recall a sent email.

items.scenario: It's your first day on an unfamiliar repository with Claude Code installed.
items.question: What's the best first move?
options: Ask it to modernise the codebase immediately
Create a branch, then ask questions about structure, build and tests before requesting any change
Switch to bypassPermissions so exploration is fast
Paste the README into chat instead
items.explanation: Questions before changes, and Git as the safety net. You learn the codebase and verify Claude's understanding before it touches anything.
distractors: Large changes before you understand the repo are risky and hard to review.
Widest permission on day one is exactly what not to do.
That throws away the repo-aware agent you have.

items.scenario: You want Claude Code to propose an approach to a risky schema migration, but you don't want any files changed yet.
items.question: Which permission mode fits?
options: acceptEdits
plan
bypassPermissions
dontAsk
items.explanation: Plan mode explores and proposes without editing, so you review the approach before execution.
distractors: acceptEdits applies file edits without asking, which is the opposite of what you want.
No checks at all. Sandbox or CI only.
dontAsk auto-denies anything not pre-allowed. It's for locked-down automation, not reviewing a plan.

items.scenario: A teammate suggests running bypassPermissions on their laptop because 'the prompts slow me down'.
items.question: What's the correct guidance?
options: Fine, as long as they're on a branch
No. bypassPermissions belongs only in an isolated sandbox or CI container. On a working laptop it can reach credentials, files and the network unchecked
Fine, as long as they use the most capable model
Fine during working hours only
items.explanation: A branch protects code, not your machine. Commands can still touch credentials, other directories and the network.
distractors: Git can't undo a leaked credential or a command run outside the repo.
Model capability doesn't remove the risk of acting unchecked, including injected instructions.
Risk doesn't depend on the clock.

items.scenario: Claude Code tells you the payment module retries failed charges three times with exponential backoff.
items.question: Before you repeat this in a design review, what should you do?
options: Nothing. Claude Code read the code, so it's correct
Open the referenced code and verify the retry logic yourself
Ask Claude Code again for confirmation
Check that the answer is formatted as a table
items.explanation: Verify key answers by reading the code. Agents can misread or generalise from a similarly named function.
distractors: Having read files isn't a guarantee of reading the right ones correctly.
Self-confirmation isn't independent verification.
Format is irrelevant to correctness.

items.scenario: A long Claude Code session has become slow and is mixing up details from an earlier, unrelated task.
items.question: What's the best action?
options: Keep going. More context is always better
Check context use with /context, then /clear to start the new task fresh (or /compact if you need continuity)
Reinstall Claude Code
Switch to bypassPermissions to speed things up
items.explanation: Unrelated history pollutes context and costs tokens. Clear between tasks, and compact when you need a summary carried forward.
distractors: Irrelevant context dilutes attention and raises cost.
This is a context problem, not an installation one.
Permissions don't affect context quality.
